title: Alcmene et Galanthis
source: P. Ovidius Naso, Metamorphoses, ed. Hugo Magnus (Gotha: F.A. Perthes), public domain; TEI from PerseusDL/canonical-latinLit phi0959.phi006.perseus-lat2, sha256 8719b7d375018d4f. Collated against The Latin Library (cltk mirror) as a disagreement detector only. Original spelling kept. Pronunciation convention: reconstructed Classical (restored) Latin, applied consistently. All translations were made fresh from the Latin for Lectorium.
about: Alcmene, Hercules’ mother and old now, has Iole to tell her griefs to, whom Hyllus has taken to wife at Hercules’ bidding and who is carrying a child. Wishing her a quick delivery, Alcmene tells her own: how the goddess set over women in labour came to her already bought by Juno, sat down on the altar before the door with her legs crossed and her fingers locked, and held the birth of Hercules back through seven days and nights while Alcmene strained, hurled abuse at Jupiter and longed to die. A servant of the house, Galanthis, guessed what was being done and broke the spell with a lie — the mistress is delivered, come and congratulate her — and the goddess, springing up in fright, undid the knot herself. For laughing at it Galanthis was dragged off by the hair and made into an animal that keeps her old quickness and the colour of her hair, and that, the tale ends, brings forth her young by the mouth.

sentences.t: Sensit Atlas pondus.—
sentences.l: Atlas felt the weight.
sentences.n: A half-line, and then a dash: the sentence closes off what has just been happening in the heavens before the poem comes down to Eurystheus and to Alcmene. Atlas holds up the sky, and what he feels is a change in its weight; Ovid says no more than that here, and the reader is left to supply the cause. sensit is the perfect of sentio, “perceive, feel” — the same verb returns at 308, of Galanthis, who also senses something she cannot see.

sentences.t:
Neque adhuc Stheneleius iras
solverat Eurystheus odiumque in prole paternum
exercebat atrox.
sentences.l: Nor had Stheneleian Eurystheus yet loosed his angers, and, savage, he kept exercising upon the offspring the hatred he bore the father.
sentences.i: Eurystheus, son of Sthenelus, had still not let his anger go: a savage man, he went on visiting upon the children the hatred he had borne their father.
sentences.n: Stheneleius is a patronymic adjective, “son of Sthenelus”, and Latin verse uses such a form in place of a name as freely as the name itself. iras is a poetic plural — one anger in many outbursts. paternum odium is best taken as the hatred aimed at the father rather than a hatred inherited from one, so that what was felt for Hercules is now spent on his line; the adjective will bear either sense and only the run of the sentence decides it. atrox stands alone at the end: the form would let it describe odium as well, but the distance from that noun and the sense of the line give it to Eurystheus. The pluperfect solverat and the imperfect exercebat together give a state that was still in force when the story opens.

sentences.t:
At longis anxia curis
Argolis Alcmene, questus ubi ponat aniles,
cui referat nati testatos orbe labores,
cuive suos casus, Iolen habet.
sentences.l: But Argive Alcmene, anxious with long cares, has Iole: somewhere to lay down her old woman’s complaints, someone to whom to recount her son’s labours, borne witness to by the world, or to whom to tell her own misfortunes.
sentences.i: But Argive Alcmene, worn with long anxiety, has Iole: someone to set an old woman’s grievances down with, someone to tell over her son’s labours — the world is their witness — or her own misfortunes.
sentences.n: Argolis is a Greek feminine adjective, “Argive”, used of a woman of Argos, and Iolen is a Greek accusative; Ovid keeps such Greek forms in his Latin, and the Greek accusative Galanthida at 316 is another. ubi ponat, cui referat and cuive are relative clauses of purpose, with the subjunctive: not “where she lays them down” but “somewhere to lay them down”, “someone to tell it to”. ubi is a word for a place, used here of a person — Iole is where the complaints can be put. testatos is the perfect participle of the deponent testor, “bear witness”; a deponent participle usually keeps its active force, but here it is used passively, “borne witness to”, with orbe the plain ablative of what did the witnessing. In the last clause referat is not repeated and has to be supplied.

sentences.t:
Herculis illam
imperiis thalamoque animoque receperat Hyllus
inpleratque uterum generoso semine, cum sic
incipit Alcmene:
sentences.l: Hyllus had received her, at Hercules’ commands, into his marriage-chamber and into his heart, and had filled her womb with noble seed, when Alcmene begins thus:
sentences.i: At Hercules’ bidding Hyllus had taken her into his marriage bed and into his heart, and had filled her womb with noble seed; and it was then that Alcmene began:
sentences.n: The two pluperfects receperat and inpleratque set the background, and then the event that matters arrives inside the cum-clause with a present verb, incipit. This is the inverted cum, where what looks like the subordinate clause carries the story forward: “...when Alcmene begins”. inpleratque is the edition’s spelling of impleverat — syncopated, and with inp- for imp-, both kept as Magnus prints them. thalamoque animoque puts the bedchamber and the heart under one verb. Magnus prints cum here; some editions print cui, “to whom”, which would give “to whom Alcmene thus begins” and make the sentence a plain statement rather than this inversion.

sentences.t:
“Faveant tibi numina saltem
conripiantque moras,
sentences.l: “May the divine powers favour you, at least, and cut short the delays,
sentences.i: “May heaven at least be good to you, and cut the waiting short,
sentences.n: Faveant and conripiant are present subjunctives standing on their own as a wish — the jussive subjunctive, “may they...”. saltem, “at least”, is the bitter word in the sentence: Alcmene is asking for Iole what she herself did not get. corripere moras is literally to snatch the delays up, corripio being a verb of seizing that Latin also uses of hurrying. numina are the divine powers as they act, not the gods as persons.

sentences.t:
tum cum matura vocabis
praepositam timidis parientibus Ilithyiam,
quam mihi difficilem Iunonis gratia fecit.
sentences.l: then, when, come to term, you shall call on Ilithyia, who is set over frightened women in labour — whom the favour of Juno made hard toward me.
sentences.i: then, when your time is full and you call on Ilithyia, who is set over women in the fear of childbirth — the goddess whom Juno’s influence turned hard against me.
sentences.n: matura is nominative and describes Iole herself, “ripe, come to full term”; it is not an adverb on the calling. praepositam takes the dative timidis parientibus, because praeponere aliquem alicui is to set someone over someone. parientibus is the present participle of pario, “give birth”, used as a noun, “those in labour”; the same participle comes back at 322, of Alcmene herself. Ilithyia is the Greek name of the birth-goddess whom Alcmene calls Lucina at 294 — Ovid uses both. Iunonis gratia is a genitive that runs either way and the Latin does not settle it: the favour Ilithyia wanted from Juno, or the favour she did her. Either way the pull is Juno’s, and the goddess who should have helped arrived already on the other side; mihi is the dative of the person it fell out badly for.

sentences.t:
Namque laboriferi cum iam natalis adesset
Herculis et decimum premeretur sidere signum,
sentences.l: For when the birth-day of toil-bearing Hercules was now at hand, and the tenth sign was being pressed by the star,
sentences.i: For when the day was already at hand that would bring toil-bearing Hercules to birth, and the star was pressing into the tenth sign,
sentences.n: laborifer is a compound adjective of the kind Latin verse makes at will, “toil-bearing”, and the labores it points at are the labours the world bore witness to at 277 — the same word will be Alcmene’s own word for her birth-pangs four lines below. natalis is the day of birth, with dies understood. The star pressing into the tenth sign is the sun, whose passage through the signs of the zodiac counts out the months; the tenth is full term, since Roman reckoning gave a pregnancy ten months. adesset and premeretur are imperfect subjunctives in a cum-clause of circumstance.

sentences.t:
tendebat gravitas uterum mihi, quodque ferebam,
tantum erat, ut posses auctorem dicere tecti
ponderis esse Iovem.
sentences.l: the heaviness was stretching my womb, and what I was carrying was so great that you could say that Jupiter was the author of the covered weight.
sentences.i: the weight of it was stretching my womb, and what I carried was so great that anyone could tell the hidden burden had Jupiter for its maker.
sentences.n: mihi is a dative of the person concerned and does the work of “my” with uterum. tantum erat, ut posses is a result clause, “so great that you could...”. posses is second person singular, but Iole was not there to see any of it, so this is the generalising “you” of “anyone would have said”. auctorem ... esse Iovem is an indirect statement inside dicere — accusative and infinitive, “that Jupiter was the author”. tectus, “covered”, is the ordinary word for something hidden away, and the weight is covered because it is still unborn. auctor is a maker or originator, used here of fathering.

sentences.t:
Nec iam tolerare labores
ulterius poteram:
sentences.l: Nor could I bear the labours any further now:
sentences.i: And I could bear the pains no longer:
sentences.n: labores is the word that stood for Hercules’ Labours at 277 and stands inside laborifer at 285; here it is what a woman goes through in bringing him into the world. Latin lets the one word carry both, and English has kept the same double sense in “labour”. ulterius is the comparative adverb, “further than this”.

sentences.t:
quin nunc quoque frigidus artus,
dum loquor, horror habet, parsque est meminisse doloris.
sentences.l: indeed even now, while I speak, a cold shudder holds my limbs, and to remember is a part of the pain.
sentences.i: indeed even now, as I speak, the cold shudder of it grips my limbs, and the remembering is itself part of the pain.
sentences.n: quin here is not the conjunction but the intensifier, “why, in fact, indeed”. frigidus and its noun horror are held apart across the line-end, with artus and dum loquor standing between them, so that the limbs and the speaking sit inside the shudder that holds them; artus is the accusative object of habet. horror is the physical bristling of the skin before it is any feeling. meminisse is a perfect infinitive with present sense, and it is the subject of est: “to remember is a part”. The sentence steps out of the story and back into the room where the two women are sitting.

sentences.t:
Septem ego per noctes, totidem cruciata diebus,
fessa malis tendensque ad caelum bracchia magno
Lucinam Nixosque pares clamore vocabam.
sentences.l: Through seven nights, and racked as many days, worn out with sufferings and stretching my arms to heaven, I kept calling on Lucina and the Nixi, her equals, with a great cry.
sentences.i: Seven nights I went through, and as many days on the rack; worn out with pain, my arms stretched up to heaven, I called and called on Lucina, and on the Nixi her equals, with a great cry.
sentences.n: cruciata is a passive participle from crucio, “rack, torture”, and agrees with ego — seven nights and seven days of it. vocabam is imperfect: not one cry but calling and calling. Lucina is the Roman name of the goddess called Ilithyia at 283. The Nixi are minor deities of childbirth, and pares says only that they are her match or her fellows; little is known of them beyond the name, and Ovid explains nothing. magno at the end of one line and clamore in the next stand wide apart with the whole naming of the gods between them, so that the cry surrounds what it calls on.

sentences.t:
Illa quidem venit, sed praecorrupta meumque
quae donare caput Iunoni vellet iniquae.
sentences.l: She came indeed, but bought beforehand, and one who would make a present of my head to unfair Juno.
sentences.i: Come she did — but bought in advance, and ready to hand my life over as a gift to unjust Juno.
sentences.n: praecorrupta is corrumpo with prae-: corrupted, bought, before ever she arrived. quae ... vellet is a relative clause with the subjunctive describing the kind of person she was, “the sort who would want to...”. caput, “head”, stands for the life itself, which is standard Latin. donare aliquid alicui is to make a present of a thing to someone, and the cruelty is in the gift-word. iniqua is “unfair, not even-handed”, and it is Alcmene’s word for Juno, spoken by the woman whose life was being handed over. The relative pronoun quae is pushed back inside meum ... caput, which Latin verse does constantly and English cannot.

sentences.t:
Utque meos audit gemitus, subsedit in illa
ante fores ara dextroque a poplite laevum
pressa genu digitis inter se pectine iunctis
sustinuit partus.
sentences.l: And as she hears my groans, she sat down on that altar before the doors and, pressed as to her left knee by the crook of the right, with her fingers joined among themselves comb-wise, she held the birth back.
sentences.i: And the moment she heard me groaning she sat down on the altar there before the doors, crossed the right leg down on the left knee, laced her fingers together like the teeth of a comb, and held the birth back.
sentences.n: The tenses shift inside the sentence: audit is a present in a past story, the historic present, which brings the moment up close, and then subsedit and sustinuit are perfects again. pressa is a passive participle used in the Greek way, with laevum genu as an accusative of the part affected — “pressed as to her left knee”; poples, the crook or back of the knee, is what does the pressing. digitis ... iunctis is an ablative absolute, “with the fingers joined”, and pectine, “with a comb”, says how: interlocked like a comb’s teeth. in illa ... ara, “on that altar”, is split around ante fores. Crossed legs and locked fingers are a binding — the goddess ties her own body into a knot and the birth cannot pass. Magnus prints no connective between genu and digitis; some editions read genu et digitis, which joins the two phrases openly and makes the line easier to construe.

sentences.t:
Tacita quoque carmina voce
dixit, et inceptos tenuerunt carmina partus.
sentences.l: She spoke charms besides in a silent voice, and the charms held back the birth already begun.
sentences.i: She said spells too, under her breath, and the spells held back a birth already under way.
sentences.n: quoque here is the adverb, “besides, as well”, and not the ablative quo with -que, “and with which” — worth checking each time the word appears. carmen is a song, and by that road a spell: words with power in them because of the way they are put together. Tacita ... voce, “with a silent voice”, is not a contradiction but the standing description of an incantation muttered too low to hear. carmina is said twice, once inside each half of the sentence, and partus, the word that ended the sentence before this one, ends this one too: the repetitions bind the sentence as the spell binds the birth. inceptos partus — the labour was already begun when it was stopped.

sentences.t:
Nitor et ingrato facio convicia demens
vana Iovi cupioque mori moturaque duros
verba queror silices.
sentences.l: I strain, and out of my senses I hurl empty abuse at ungrateful Jupiter, and I long to die, and I make complaint in words that would move hard flint.
sentences.i: I bear down; out of my mind, I fling useless abuse at Jupiter for his ingratitude; I long to die; and I pour out words that would have moved hard flint.
sentences.n: nitor, “I push, I strain”, is the verb that stands behind the name of the Nixi she called on at 294 — the straining gods, and now the straining woman. All four verbs are present in a past story, the historic present, which is why the pains are happening as she tells them. convicia, abuse shouted at someone, takes the dative ingrato ... Iovi: ungrateful is Alcmene’s charge against the father of the child, hers and not the poem’s, and the poem lets her make it. demens is “out of one’s mind”, and it stands beside vana, “empty”: she knows the abuse is useless while she is shouting it. motura is a future participle agreeing with verba — words “about to move”, that is, such as would move; silices are flints, the hardest thing there is to shift.

sentences.t:
Matres Cadmeides adsunt
votaque suscipiunt exhortanturque dolentem.
sentences.l: The Cadmean mothers stand by, and take up vows and hearten the one in pain.
sentences.i: The mothers of Thebes stand by; they take vows upon themselves and hearten the woman in her pain.
sentences.n: Cadmeides is another Greek feminine plural, “daughters of Cadmus”, that is, the women of Thebes, the city Cadmus founded. vota suscipere is the set phrase for taking a vow upon oneself: promising a god something in return for what is asked. exhortantur is deponent — passive in ending, active in meaning, “they encourage”. dolentem, “the one grieving, the one in pain”, is Alcmene herself, and she says it in the third person: for a moment she is looking at herself from where the other women stood. She does the same again at 322.

sentences.t:
Una ministrarum, media de plebe, Galanthis,
flava comas, aderat, faciendis strenua iussis,
officiis dilecta suis.
sentences.l: One of the serving-women, from the common sort, Galanthis, yellow as to her hair, was there, brisk for orders to be carried out, loved for her services.
sentences.i: One of the maids was there — Galanthis, of common stock, yellow-haired, quick to do what she was told, and loved for her service.
sentences.n: flava comas is the Greek accusative of respect: the adjective is nominative and describes her, and the accusative comas says in what respect — “golden, as to her hair”. Keep the colour in mind; it comes back at 320. faciendis ... iussis is a gerundive in the dative after strenua, orders “to be carried out”, so: brisk for the doing of them. media de plebe, “from the middle of the common people”, places her exactly, a servant of no rank — and it is she, not the Theban matrons, who does something. officiis ... suis is an ablative of cause with dilecta, loved for her services.

sentences.t:
Ea sensit iniqua
nescio quid Iunone geri,
sentences.l: She felt that something or other was being done, with Juno unfair,
sentences.i: She sensed that something was afoot, with Juno unjust behind it —
sentences.n: nescio quid is a fossil: “I do not know what”, welded into a single indefinite, “something or other”. geri is a present passive infinitive in indirect statement after sensit — she perceived that something was being carried on. iniqua Iunone can be read two ways, and both are good Latin: as an ablative absolute, “Juno being unfair”, which is how it is taken here, or as a bare ablative of the agent, “by unfair Juno”, without the ab that prose would want. sensit is the verb this part opened with at 273, and a servant now does what Atlas did.

sentences.t:
dumque exit et intrat
saepe fores, divam residentem vidit in ara
bracchiaque in genibus digitis conexa tenentem,
sentences.l: and while she goes out and comes in at the doors often, she saw the goddess sitting on the altar and holding her arms, linked by the fingers, upon her knees,
sentences.i: and, in and out of the doorway as she often was, she caught sight of the goddess seated on the altar, her arms on her knees and her fingers laced together,
sentences.n: dum, “while”, takes the present indicative even when the story around it is in the past: exit and intrat are presents inside a perfect narrative, and English wants a past for it, “was going in and out”. fores, the double door, is the accusative of the way gone through. residentem and tenentem are present participles agreeing with divam, both governed by vidit — she saw her sitting and holding. This is the posture of 298–299 described a second time: once as Alcmene knows it now, once as her servant saw it from the doorway. conexa is the edition’s spelling, with one n.

sentences.t:
et “quaecumque es,” ait “dominae gratare: levata est
Argolis Alcmene potiturque puerpera voto.”
sentences.l: and “whoever you are,” she says, “congratulate my mistress: Argive Alcmene is lightened of her burden, and as a woman in childbed she gains what she prayed for.”
sentences.i: and “whoever you are,” she says, “wish my mistress joy: Argive Alcmene is delivered, and the new mother has what she prayed for.”
sentences.n: gratare is the imperative of grator, a deponent — passive in ending, active in meaning, “offer your congratulations” — with dominae in the dative as the person congratulated. quaecumque es, “whoever you are”, is exactly right in the mouth of a girl who has found an unknown woman sitting on the altar, and it is what disarms the goddess. levata est is “has been lightened”, relieved of the weight the sentence at 287 described, and the same root returns at 315 and 318. potitur takes the ablative voto: she gets possession of the thing prayed for, and votum is the word the Theban women’s vows were called by at 305. puerpera is a woman who has just given birth. Every word of it is false when she says it.

sentences.t:
Exsiluit iunctasque manus pavefacta remisit
diva potens uteri: vinclis levor ipsa remissis.
sentences.l: She leapt up and, struck with fear, let go her joined hands — the goddess who has power over the womb; and, with the bonds released, I myself am lightened.
sentences.i: The goddess whose power is over the womb sprang up in fright and let her locked hands fall apart; and with the bonds loosed, I myself was lightened.
sentences.n: The subject is held back to the far end of the sentence, after two verbs have already happened: diva potens uteri, “the goddess mighty over the womb”, with potens taking the genitive of what she has power over. pavefacta is “made afraid”, a compound of facio of the kind Latin builds at will. vinclis ... remissis is an ablative absolute, “with the bonds released”, and it uses the same verb as remisit two words earlier: she lets her hands go, and by that the woman is let go. levor is a passive present, “I am lightened”, the same root as levata est at 312. The bonds were never rope — the goddess’s own crossed limbs were the knot.

sentences.t: Numine decepto risisse Galanthida fama est:
sentences.l: The report is that Galanthis laughed, with the divine power tricked:
sentences.i: The story goes that Galanthis laughed at having fooled a god:
sentences.n: fama est governs an indirect statement: risisse, the perfect infinitive, with Galanthida as its accusative subject. Galanthida is the Greek accusative of the Greek name, kept as Greek. Numine decepto is an ablative absolute, “the divine power having been deceived”. fama est is not filler: Alcmene is telling this at second hand, because she was behind those doors and in labour, and did not see the girl laugh.

sentences.t:
ridentem prensamque ipsis dea saeva capillis
traxit,
sentences.l: Her, laughing and caught by the very hair, the savage goddess dragged,
sentences.i: The savage goddess had her by the hair, laughing still, and dragged her,
sentences.n: ridentem and prensam are accusative participles with no noun to lean on: the girl herself has to be supplied, as often in Latin verse, and English needs a pronoun for it. ipsis ... capillis is an ablative of the means, “by the hair itself”, ipse marking that the hair and nothing else was what held her. saeva, “savage”, is Alcmene’s word for the goddess, not the poem’s — everything from 281 onward is inside her speech to Iole.

sentences.t:
et e terra corpus relevare volentem
arcuit inque pedes mutavit bracchia primos.
sentences.l: and, as she wished to lift her body up from the earth, blocked her, and changed her arms into front feet.
sentences.i: and when she wanted to raise herself from the ground the goddess kept her from it, and turned her arms into forefeet.
sentences.n: volentem is a third accusative participle for the same unnamed girl, and it is the object of arcuit: “her, wanting to lift her body, she kept off”. arceo is to fend off or shut out — the goddess does not strike her, she simply will not let her get up. relevare puts the lev- root here for the third time: the goddess who would not lighten a woman in labour will not let this one lift herself. pedes primos are the “first feet”, the front pair, and the phrase quietly tells you how many there now are.

sentences.t:
Strenuitas antiqua manet, nec terga colorem
amisere suum: forma est diversa priori.
sentences.l: Her old briskness stays, and her back has not lost its colour; her shape is different from the one before.
sentences.i: The old quickness stays with her, and her back keeps the colour it had; her shape is different now from what it was.
sentences.n: strenuitas is built on the strenua of 307: the quality the girl was praised for is the quality the animal keeps. The colour that stays is the flava of 307 as well, the yellow of her hair, now on an animal’s back. amisere is amiserunt, the poetic third-person plural perfect in -ere that verse uses constantly; it sits here beside the full form tenuerunt at 301, the same tense in two endings, each chosen for its line. terga is a plural for one back. diversa takes the dative priori, “different from the earlier one”. Ovid does not name the creature.

sentences.t:
Quae quia mendaci parientem iuverat ore,
ore parit nostrasque domos, ut et ante, frequentat.”
sentences.l: And she, because she had helped a woman in labour with a lying mouth, gives birth by the mouth, and haunts our houses, as she did before as well.”
sentences.i: And because it was with a lying mouth that she helped a woman in labour, by the mouth she brings forth her young; and she is about our houses still, as she was before.”
sentences.n: Quae is a connecting relative — a relative pronoun standing where English puts “and she”, opening a new sentence rather than a subordinate clause. ore closes one line and opens the next, in the same case and the same form, and that repetition is the whole argument: a mouth for a mouth, the punishment made out of the offence. parientem is the participle of 283 again, now singular, and it is Alcmene speaking of herself from outside for the second time. Ovid gives the creature no name here and makes no claim about the girl’s name: what he offers is this one account of how it bears its young. The present tenses parit and frequentat carry the story out of Alcmene’s past and into an unfinished present, and ut et ante says she is still in service.
